1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once and claims a share of the centre. The cost is the pawn chain on e6 and d5, which shuts in the light-squared bishop on c8, and Black usually looks for counterplay by hitting White's centre at its base with ...c5. White chooses how to hold or release the tension, so the game can become closed or open.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Bb4+.strategy: Checks at once but gains nothing: 3.c3 drives the bishop back with a useful move, and 3.Bd2 offers a trade that helps White's development. Black loses time and has not yet challenged the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.name: French Defence: St. George Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.background: The name is borrowed from the St. George Defence, 1.e4 a6, named after England's patron saint, which reaches this position with 2.d4 e6. Its first known game is a simultaneous one in which the English amateur J. Baker beat Wilhelm Steinitz on 11 December 1868.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.strategy: Keeps a White bishop off b5 and prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7 against e4, while Black can still build a French-style centre. The cost is a tempo on a rim pawn move, and White can answer by taking space and developing freely. It leads to an unorthodox game in which Black hopes to attack the centre from the wing.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchet the queen's bishop against e4, but it lets White's two central pawns stand unchallenged. White can support e4, develop and keep the larger centre, and Black's pieces have little to hit.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5.name: French Defence: Franco-Sicilian Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and aims to trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, with ...e6 already played. White can give extra space or open the game. A rare sideline, not refuted but less sound than challenging the centre at once with the d-pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d6.name: Rat Defence: Small Centre Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d6.strategy: Keeps the centre compact with pawns on e6 and d6 and aims for quick development and castling, with a pawn break in the centre later. Without ...d5 Black stays passive and White can take more space or develop freely.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops and presses on d4, but blocks the c7-pawn, so the usual French break ...c5 against d4 is no longer at hand. White keeps more space and can even drive the knight back with d5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 or c7, but on a6 the knight stands offside and does nothing against the centre. White can take b4 away with 3.a3 and keeps the larger centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qe7.strategy: Puts the queen in front of the f8 bishop and takes e7 from the knight, yet does nothing to challenge the centre. White develops freely and keeps the space advantage.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qf6.strategy: Brings the queen out early against d4 and takes f6 from the knight. White develops with gain of time, for instance 3.Nc3 with Nd5 or e5 to follow against the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qh4.strategy: Attacks the e4-pawn, but White defends it with a developing move, and gains more time later by attacking the queen with a knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly before ...d5 and leaves g7 without its defender, so 3.Qg4 attacks it at once. Otherwise White keeps the larger centre with simple development, as the bishop on e7 does not bear on d4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d7-pawn, so ...d5 is impossible for now, and puts the bishop on a square that 3.e5 attacks at once. Taking on e5 gives the bishop for a pawn after dxe5, so it retreats, and White has gained space and time.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where e4 and the queen cover its forward squares f5 and g4, so it does nothing against the centre. White develops freely and keeps the larger centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nf6.name: French Defence: Mediterranean Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 but allows 3.e5, which drives the knight away: after 3...Nd5 4.c4 it has to move a third time, and White has gained space and time before Black has played ...d5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8 bishop, which can come out only after ...g6 or once the knight moves on, and puts no pressure on d4 or e4. White develops freely and keeps the larger centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a wing move that neither develops a piece nor challenges the centre, and weakens b5. White uses the time to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a pawn triangle on c6, d5 and e6 that shuts in the c8 bishop, which cannot come out to f5. White can then close the centre with e5 and gain space, and Black's ...c5 break costs a second tempo.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Takes e5 and prepares ...e5, but opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 3.Qh5+ forces ...g6 or ...Ke7, and the king loses its cover. The pawn also takes the best square from the knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5.name: French Defence: Franco-Hiva Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5.strategy: Attacks e4 in Dutch style, but after 3.exf5 exf5 the e-file and the e8-h5 diagonal lie open in front of Black's king, and the f5-pawn needs defending against Bd3. White develops quickly, and Black has no compensation for the loosened position.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 against d4, but with pawns on e6 and g6 the dark squares f6 and h6 are weak, and h4 followed by h5 can strike at g6. Otherwise White simply takes the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 h6.strategy: A prophylactic move against Bg5 that is not yet needed, since the queen would simply take the bishop. It spends a tempo on a rim pawn, so White develops with time to spare, but it does no real harm.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and g6 for good and neither develops a piece nor challenges the centre. White uses the tempo to develop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Qg5.strategy: Hangs the queen: the bishop's diagonal c1-g5 is open after d4, and 3.Bxg5 wins her for nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the f8 bishop. 3.Bg5+ follows at once, and Black must block or move the king again, so it stays stuck in the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop en prise to the d-pawn: 3.dxc5 wins it, and no Black piece can recapture.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.Nxa3 or 3.bxa3 takes it, and nothing recaptures, so Black is a whole piece down.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 b5.name: French Defence: Baeuerle Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for play on the long diagonal with ...Bb7. After 3.Bxb5 Bb7 White can defend e4 and keep the extra pawn, as Black's activity hardly compensates.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 g5.strategy: Weakens the kingside for nothing: after 3.Nf3 the pawn is attacked by knight and bishop and defended only by the queen, so Black must defend or advance it and loses time and structure.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Pushes the e-pawn a second time straight into 3.dxe5, and no Black piece can recapture at once. Black has spent two moves on the e-pawn only to give it up.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and guards d4 and e5, keeping the pawn centre flexible instead of committing the c-pawn. It prepares the bishop on d3 and castling, and leaves Black to show whether the queenside advance is really worth the loosening.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Three Pawn Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a broad three-pawn centre at once and prepares to punish the queenside advance that Black's last move invites: after ...b5 White takes, and the recaptured pawn on b5 stands loose. The price is that the centre is built before any piece is out, so the pawns need support.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and guards e4, the plain way to build the centre. Here it is less secure than it looks: a knight on c3 meets ...b5 and ...b4, which drives it off and takes the defender from e4, so Black gains queenside space with tempo. Playable, but it lets Black's last move pay off.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Sanky-George Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5.strategy: A gambit: Black strikes at the c4 pawn and, if White takes, recaptures so as to open the a-file, but the pawn on b5 is then loose and the bishop can win it. An open file and quick development are real but modest compensation, so this is an offbeat try, not a solid choice.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 at once, the natural answer to a white centre. With a pawn on c4 as well, the trades on d5 come quickly and open the game; if Black's queen has to recapture, White gains time against it, so the development must be accurate, but the pawns stay level and Black has no weakness.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 with a flank pawn, but White simply pushes d5 and gains space, with the pawns on c4 and e4 backing it up. Black's pieces are short of squares and White keeps a lasting edge, so the flank pawn costs Black the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5.strategy: Accepts the gambit, the principal answer: White takes the pawn and, after Black's recapture, can win the loose pawn on b5 with the f1-bishop. The price is some time, since Black gets an open a-file against the a2 pawn, so White has to consolidate carefully.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and guards e4 instead of taking the pawn: if Black takes on c4, Bxc4 regains it at once with the centre intact. The weakness is ...b4, which drives the knight off and leaves e4 unguarded, so the move gives Black time and a choice. Playable, but it passes up the principled capture.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and leaves the tension: if Black takes on c4, Bxc4 regains the pawn at once. The knight does not guard e4, though, so ...Bb7 attacks the pawn immediately and White has to spend a move on its defence before it can think of capturing on b5. Playable, but it gives Black the choice of how the fight goes.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5 axb5.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, St. George Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5 axb5.strategy: The natural recapture and the point of the gambit: the a-pawn leaves the a-file, so the rook looks at a2, and White must decide whether the loose pawn on b5 is worth taking. Not recapturing would leave Black a pawn down for nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5 c6.strategy: Offers a second pawn for open lines instead of recapturing: White takes on a6 or on c6 and simply stays a pawn up. The only return is some activity on the queenside, which does not make up for the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5 Bb7.strategy: Develops the bishop against e4 before recapturing, which keeps the a-file and the long diagonal in play. White can support e4 first, and after ...axb5 the game is much the same pawn-down gambit. Sound, but no more accurate than recapturing at once.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5.strategy: The idea of the whole set-up: Black grabs queenside space and prepares ...Bb7 against e4. But it loosens the queenside before any piece is out, and White can attack the advanced pawn at once, keeping a clear edge. Playable, but it hands White the easier game.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: The sound way to meet 3.Nf3: Black challenges e4 at once, and the spare ...a6 does no harm, since it keeps a white bishop off b5 and prepares the queenside advance. Black gets a solid pawn chain and an easy game; the tempo spent on ...a6 costs little.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and aims for an open game with ...a6 already played, trading the solid pawn chain for freer pieces. White chooses whether to open the centre or support d4, and Black has not challenged e4, so White decides the character of the game. Sound, but offbeat.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3.strategy: Puts the bishop on its natural diagonal, guarding e4 in advance against ...Bb7 and eyeing b5. A sensible set-up, but it leaves Black free to hit the centre with ...c5 and ...Bb7, so White keeps only a small edge.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Nbd2.strategy: Guards e4 with a piece before the black bishop reaches b7, keeping the structure compact and the f1-bishop free to choose its square. The knight shuts in the c1-bishop for now, but it is a sound set-up that keeps White's edge.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.a4.strategy: Hits the b5 pawn twice, with the a-pawn and the f1-bishop, so Black must deal with it at once. It costs a tempo on the flank, but it takes the sting out of the queenside advance and keeps White's edge.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Black challenges the centre instead of waiting behind it: the d4 pawn is now attacked by the c-pawn and held only by the knight, because the bishop on d3 shuts in the queen. White has to decide how to meet the tension, and Black gets active play before castling.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 Bb7.strategy: Brings the bishop to the long diagonal against e4, the point of the queenside advance. The bishop on d3 is tied to guarding the pawn, and Black keeps every way of challenging the centre open, so White's set-up has to be accurate.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight with a hit at e4, which the bishop holds. Without the bishop on b7 the pressure is mild, so White can gain space with e5: the knight is driven to d5 and Black has handed White a central wedge. Playable, but it lets White set the structure.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Adds a second defender to d4 and keeps the centre intact instead of releasing the tension by capturing on c5. The price is that the queen's knight loses its natural square and has to come out via d2, but White keeps a solid pawn chain and the bishop on its diagonal.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.O-O.strategy: Gets the king safe and a rook ready before the centre opens, and leaves the d4 pawn to be traded. If Black takes on d4, the knight recaptures to the centre with active pieces; if not, c3 can still follow. A sound alternative that leaves Black the choice of releasing the tension.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.dxc5.strategy: Resolves the tension at once, trading the central d-pawn for Black's c-pawn. After ...Bxc5 the d4 pawn needs no more defending, but the bishop becomes active on the diagonal towards f2 and White is left with a single central pawn. Sound but unambitious.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal against e4, which is what the queenside advance was for. The pawn is held by the bishop on d3, so for now this is pressure, not a threat, but every further attacker on e4 makes it one.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 N.strategy: Develops and piles on d4, but the knight walks into d5: the pawn attacks it with tempo, and Black's pieces end up short of room behind a white space gain. White is clearly better, so the pressure on d4 costs more than it gains.

Develops with an immediate hit at e4, held once by the bishop. White can answer by gaining space with e5, when the knight must go to d5 and the pressure on e4 is gone. Playable, but it gives White the central wedge and the choice of set-up.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.strategy: Gets the king to safety before the centre opens. With Black's bishop already aimed at e4 and the d4 pawn under pressure, White wants the king out of the middle and a rook developed, while the bishop and the pawn chain hold the centre together for now.
Adds a second defender of e4 and so meets ...Nf6 in advance, keeping the knight on b1 free to choose its square. It delays castling, and ...c4 can then gain space by driving the bishop from d3.

Defends e4 with a piece, the simplest way to hold the pawn against the coming ...Nf6. The knight on d2 shuts in the c1-bishop and is a little passive, and the king still has to castle, but the centre stays solid.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Traditional Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.strategy: Brings out the last minor piece with a point: e4 is now attacked twice, by bishop and knight, and defended once, so White has to defend or advance the pawn at once. Black develops while keeping the initiative against the white centre and the space gained on the queenside.

Develops and piles on d4, but White answers d5, which hits the knight and shuts the long diagonal. The knight must retreat and Black's pieces are cramped, so the pressure on d4 gives White a clear advantage.

Resolves the tension: after cxd4 cxd4 White has the ideal pawn pair on d4 and e4, but the c-file is open for Black and e4 is still under pressure from the bishop. Black hands White the big centre in return for targets to attack; reasonable, but less ambitious than keeping the tension.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5 3.d5.name: Benoni Defence: French Benoni
1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5 3.d5.strategy: Gains space and attacks e6, though the pawn there is defended twice and nothing is lost. If Black trades on d5, the e-file opens and White's pawn on d5 takes the c6 and e6 squares from Black's pieces; if Black does not, White has a cramping wedge in the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5 3.Nf3.strategy: The principled answer: White defends d4 with a developing move and keeps the choice of centre. If Black takes on d4, the knight recaptures and White has an open game with the central pawn and more space; if Black does not, d4 is held without any weakening.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 c5 3.c3.strategy: Props up d4 with a pawn instead of a piece, aiming for a solid centre. Black can strike at e4 with the d-pawn at once, and the queen's knight loses its natural square, but White keeps a sound, flexible structure and the choice between holding d4 and recapturing on it.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5 3.exf5.name: French Defence: Franco-Hiva Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5 3.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn, the right answer to a move that develops nothing and weakens the king's diagonal. If Black recaptures with the e-pawn, the e-file and the e8–h5 diagonal are open in front of the king, and White simply develops with the easier game.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 by developing instead of taking on f5. If Black captures on e4, White can recapture or offer the pawn again for quick development, and the loosened kingside gives White targets. White keeps a small but lasting edge.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 f5 3.e5.strategy: Closes the centre and gains space, taking the f6 square away from Black's knight. The chain can be undermined from its base and its head, so White gets a space edge but no clear advantage, and Black has a clear plan to play for.
